title: test-0029-SOC-HIS-COUNTRYSIDE
passage: In the mid-19th century, Bengal was gripped by the Blue Rebellion, a fierce uprising where ryots (peasants) refused to grow indigo. Unlike the common belief that indigo was a synthetic chemical, it was a natural dye extracted from plants grown in the fertile soil of India. The British planters forced farmers into contracts, offering cash advances that trapped them in a cycle of debt rather than wealth. Under the 'Nij' system, planters did not plough the fields themselves; they hired labourers or forced ryots to do the backbreaking work on land they directly controlled. Many farmers were reluctant to switch to indigo because it exhausted the soil, making it impossible to grow rice afterwards. Meanwhile, the Permanent Settlement had turned zamindars into landlords, yet they often lost their estates if they failed to pay the fixed revenue to the British on time. The rebellion was not a conflict between different groups of Indian farmers, but a united stand by ryots against the oppressive British planters. This struggle highlighted that the colonial revenue systems were designed to extract maximum profit, often leaving the actual cultivators in deep poverty and misery.
summary: In the mid-19th century, Bengal was gripped by the Blue Rebellion, a fierce uprising where ryots (peasants) refused to grow indigo. The rebellion wasn't between different groups of farmers, but it was a united fight by the ryots against the British planters.
